analysis.one_liner: Requires federal agencies to pay landowners when endangered species rules cut property value in half.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in February 1999 with no cosponsors, sent to the House Natural Resources Committee, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Endangered Species Act so that any federal action protecting endangered species that reduces the value of part of a private property by half or more triggers a government payout to the owner — either cash compensation or a forced buyout at pre-restriction prices, ignoring the species presence. Owners could choose binding arbitration or sue, with attorneys' fees and appraisal costs added on top. It would also create a Species Conservation Fund for buying private habitat and cap the mitigation landowners can be required to provide.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of large private parcels — especially those holding timber, mineral, oil and gas, or development rights — would gain a new right to federal payment whenever species protections halve a piece of their land's value, plus attorneys' fees and litigation costs if they win in court. Developers and resource extractors would also benefit indirectly, because agencies facing automatic payouts would have strong reason to avoid restrictions on private habitat in the first place.

how_it_helps.text: Agencies would have to either pay owners for any loss in value of 50% or more of a portion of their property, or buy that portion at pre-action fair market value with no adjustment for the endangered species present [S2] [S3].
Owners who sue and prevail would recover just compensation plus reasonable attorneys' fees, litigation costs, and appraisal fees, and could elect binding arbitration instead of court [S2] [S3].

The bill caps required mitigation: agencies could not require mitigation exceeding the scope of the harmed activity, and for land could not require more acreage than was impacted or expenditures beyond the cost of fencing and preserving the land's current condition [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund the payouts and buyouts from the responsible agency's own appropriations — a cost that would pressure agencies to weaken habitat protections rather than pay. The broader public would bear the loss of diminished endangered species and habitat protection on private land, since the bill prices habitat restrictions at full compensation and shrinks mitigation requirements.

drawbacks.text: The compensation mandate would make protecting habitat on private land dramatically more expensive, giving agencies a fiscal reason to avoid listing decisions and restrictions that affect property values — weakening the core protection of the Endangered Species Act [S2] [S3].

Buyout values would be set with no regard for the presence or use of an endangered species, and 'just compensation' would include compounded interest from the date of the taking, so payments could far exceed typical takings awards [S3].

Even supporters of property rights would have to acknowledge the open-ended fiscal exposure: payments come out of agency operating appropriations, potentially crowding out the agencies' own conservation work [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver a real benefit to a narrow group — landowners hit by severe value losses from species rules — and its compensation mechanism is a fairer way to spread a cost that regulation currently forces a few owners to absorb alone. But the design goes well beyond that: attorney's fees, compounded interest, species-blind buyout prices, and mitigation caps would make habitat protection on private land prohibitively costly, shifting the burden onto taxpayers and the species themselves. The 50% trigger plus full-fee litigation would likely deter agencies from acting rather than pay.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote for the rest of the Congress.

narrative.text: Rep. William Thomas introduced the bill on February 2, 1999, and it was referred to the House Committee on Resources [S5].
The committee took no further action, and the bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, existing Endangered Species Act habitat protections on private land remained intact and agencies faced no new compensation obligations. Conservation-minded taxpayers and the species themselves came out ahead; large landowners gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. William M. Thomas
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Endangered Species Land Management Reform Act on February 2, 1999 and delivered introductory remarks [S5].

against.name: House Committee on Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to itself on the day of introduction and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it [S5].

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill attracted zero cosponsors, so no partisan divide ever formed in the record.

industries.industry: Large private landowners, developers, and resource extractors (timber, mining, oil and gas)
industries.note: The bill would have created a right to compensation or species-blind buyouts whenever species protections halve a portion of property value, and its definitions explicitly cover timber, mineral, oil and gas, and water rights as compensable property [S3]. The same payout mandate would pressure agencies to soften habitat protections, shifting conservation costs onto the public [S2].
Compensation mandates, mitigation caps, and species-blind valuation would make protecting habitat on private land far more expensive and legally risky, reducing conservation outcomes [S2] [S3].

Agencies would gain a Species Conservation Fund for habitat acquisition but would have to pay takings claims out of their own operating appropriations, with attorneys' fees and compounded interest on top — an open-ended liability [S2] [S3].
